image.title: SDO:AIA Full-Disk View of Launching Filament

notes.naming: From Old English sunne; the Latin sol survives in 'solar'. Named long before naming conventions existed — every culture named it first.
notes.atmosphere: Not applicable — the Sun is a ball of plasma: about 73% hydrogen and 25% helium by mass, fusing ~600 million tonnes of hydrogen per second.
notes.features: The photosphere with its sunspot cycle; the million-degree corona visible during eclipses; flares and coronal mass ejections that drive space weather.
notes.missions: SOHO (1995), Parker Solar Probe (2018, first spacecraft to fly through the corona), Solar Orbiter (2020).

notes.naming: Named by the Romans for the fleet-footed messenger god, because it moves fastest across the sky.
notes.atmosphere: Essentially none — a vanishingly thin exosphere of oxygen, sodium, hydrogen, helium and potassium blasted off the surface by the solar wind.
notes.features: The 1,550-km Caloris impact basin; lobate scarps from the planet's slow shrinking; water ice in permanently shadowed polar craters.

trek.credit: NASA Mercury Trek / MESSENGER MDIS mosaic (NASA/JHUAPL/CIW)

notes.naming: Named for the Roman goddess of love and beauty — the brightest planet in the sky, the ancient morning and evening star.
notes.atmosphere: Crushing: ~96.5% carbon dioxide, 3.5% nitrogen, with sulfuric-acid clouds; surface pressure 92 times Earth's and a runaway-greenhouse surface hot enough to melt lead.
notes.features: Maxwell Montes (11 km high); thousands of volcanoes including Maat Mons; pancake domes and coronae unique to Venus; retrograde rotation slower than its year.
notes.missions: Venera 7 (first landing on another planet, 1970), Pioneer Venus, Magellan (radar-mapped 98% of the surface, 1990-94), Venus Express, Akatsuki.

trek.credit: NASA Venus Trek / Magellan SAR mosaic (NASA/JPL)

image.title: Most Amazing High Definition Image of Earth - Blue Marble 2012

notes.naming: The one planet not named from Greco-Roman myth: from Old English eorþe, simply 'ground, soil'.
notes.atmosphere: 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen — the oxygen entirely biological in origin — with argon, ~0.04% carbon dioxide and variable water vapour.
notes.features: The only known liquid-water oceans (71% of the surface), active plate tectonics, a strong magnetic field, and the only known life.
notes.missions: Home. Observed continuously by thousands of satellites since Sputnik (1957); the Apollo 8 'Earthrise' and Voyager 'Pale Blue Dot' images reframed it.

image.title: Mars Global Coverage by Context Camera on MRO

notes.naming: Named for the Roman god of war, for its blood-red colour — iron oxide dust. The month of March and the word 'martial' share the root.
notes.atmosphere: Thin: ~95% carbon dioxide, 2.8% nitrogen, 2% argon; surface pressure under 1% of Earth's; seasonal CO2 frost caps and planet-wide dust storms.
notes.features: Olympus Mons, the tallest volcano in the Solar System (~22 km); the 4,000-km Valles Marineris canyon; ancient river valleys and lakebeds; polar ice caps.
notes.missions: Mariner 4 (first flyby, 1965), Viking 1-2 (first landings, 1976), Pathfinder/Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity, Curiosity (2012-), Perseverance and the Ingenuity helicopter (2021-).

notes.naming: Named for the king of the Roman gods — fittingly, the largest planet.
notes.atmosphere: About 90% hydrogen and 10% helium with traces of methane and ammonia; banded clouds, and no solid surface anywhere.
notes.features: The Great Red Spot, a storm wider than Earth raging for centuries; the strongest planetary magnetic field; faint rings; the four Galilean moons.
notes.missions: Pioneer 10/11, Voyager 1/2 (1979), Galileo (orbited 1995-2003, dropped an atmospheric probe), Juno (2016-), Europa Clipper and JUICE en route.

notes.naming: Named for the Roman god of agriculture and time, father of Jupiter; 'Saturday' is his day.
notes.atmosphere: ~96% hydrogen, 3% helium; the least dense planet — it would float in a sufficiently large ocean.
notes.features: The great ring system, mostly water ice, spanning 280,000 km yet often under 100 m thick; the hexagonal polar jet stream; 200+ moons including haze-shrouded Titan and geysering Enceladus.
notes.missions: Pioneer 11, Voyager 1/2, Cassini-Huygens (orbited 2004-17; Huygens landed on Titan, the most distant landing ever).

image.title: Uranus as seen by NASA Voyager 2

notes.naming: The Greek primordial sky god, father of Cronus (Saturn) — the only planet named from Greek rather than Roman myth, chosen to extend the generational sequence.
notes.atmosphere: Hydrogen and helium over ~2% methane, which absorbs red light and paints the planet pale cyan; the coldest planetary atmosphere measured, down to -224 °C.
notes.features: Rolls around the Sun on its side — axial tilt 98° — probably from a giant impact; faint dark rings; 28 known moons named for Shakespeare and Pope characters.
notes.missions: Voyager 2 only (1986 flyby); a dedicated Uranus orbiter is the top-priority flagship recommendation of the 2023-2032 US planetary decadal survey.

discovery.by: Johann Galle, from Urbain Le Verrier's prediction

notes.naming: Named for the Roman god of the sea, for its deep-blue colour — fittingly, the planet found by mathematics rather than by chance.
notes.atmosphere: Hydrogen, helium and methane; the fastest winds in the Solar System, over 2,000 km/h.
notes.features: The Great Dark Spot seen by Voyager 2 (since vanished); five faint rings with arcs; Triton, a captured Kuiper-belt world orbiting backwards with nitrogen geysers.
notes.missions: Voyager 2 only (1989 flyby) — every close-up image of Neptune humanity has comes from that single encounter.

image.title: Three Views of Pluto
image.credit: NASA/Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory/Southwest Research Institute

notes.naming: Named in 1930 for the Roman god of the underworld — suggested by eleven-year-old Venetia Burney of Oxford; the first two letters honour Percival Lowell.
notes.atmosphere: A thin, seasonal nitrogen atmosphere with methane and carbon monoxide that partially freezes out as Pluto recedes from the Sun.
notes.features: The bright nitrogen-ice heart, Sputnik Planitia; water-ice mountains; possible cryovolcanoes; a moon, Charon, half its own size.
notes.missions: New Horizons (2015 flyby — the images that turned a point of light into a world).

image.title: The Far Side of the Moon -- And All the Way Around

notes.naming: From Old English mōna. The Latin luna survives in 'lunar'; capitalised Moon distinguishes ours from all the others named after it.
notes.atmosphere: A negligible exosphere of argon, helium, neon and sodium — collisions between its atoms are rare.
notes.features: Dark basaltic maria ('seas') on the near side; the heavily cratered farside highlands; the South Pole–Aitken basin; permanently shadowed polar craters holding water ice.
notes.missions: Luna 2 (first impact, 1959), Apollo 11-17 (12 humans on foot, 1969-72), Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (2009-), Chang'e 4 (first farside landing, 2019), Artemis (upcoming crewed return).

trek.credit: NASA Moon Trek / LRO WAC mosaic (NASA/GSFC/ASU)

image.title: Color Map of Ceres Elliptical Projection

notes.naming: Named for the Roman goddess of agriculture and harvests — 'cereal' shares the root. Discovered by Giuseppe Piazzi on 1 January 1801.
notes.atmosphere: None to speak of; transient water vapour has been detected escaping its surface.
notes.features: The brilliant salt deposits of Occator crater; the lonely 4-km mountain Ahuna Mons, likely a cryovolcano; a possible relict subsurface briny layer.
notes.missions: Dawn (orbited 2015-18 — the first spacecraft to orbit two different extraterrestrial bodies).

notes.naming: Named for the Greek goddess of strife and discord — aptly, since its 2005 discovery forced the debate that demoted Pluto.
notes.atmosphere: Any atmosphere is currently frozen to the surface; one may form near perihelion, centuries from now.
notes.features: Slightly more massive than Pluto though marginally smaller; among the most reflective bodies known, coated in fresh methane ice; one known moon, Dysnomia.
notes.missions: None — at roughly 96 AU at discovery, it is one of the most distant objects ever found orbiting the Sun.

notes.naming: Named for the Hawaiian goddess of childbirth, honouring the observatory on Mauna Kea; its moons Hiʻiaka and Namaka are her daughters.
notes.features: Spins in under four hours — fastest of any large body — stretching it into an egg shape; has a ring, the first found around a trans-Neptunian object; crystalline water ice surface.

notes.naming: Named for the creator god of the Rapa Nui of Easter Island — discovered just after Easter 2005, and nicknamed 'Easterbunny' before formal naming.
notes.atmosphere: None detected at present; possibly transient near perihelion.
notes.features: A reddish surface of frozen methane and ethane; one known small, dark moon (MK2).

regions.name: Asteroid belt
regions.note: Millions of rocky bodies between Mars and Jupiter; Ceres, inside it, is the only dwarf planet of the inner Solar System.

regions.name: Kuiper belt
regions.note: Icy bodies beyond Neptune, including Pluto, Haumea and Makemake; Eris orbits mostly beyond it, in the scattered disc.
